newsitem.title: ZAIRE: U.N. envoy, OAU team meet Rwandan strongman.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy, OAU team meet Rwandan strongman.

text.p: A U.N. refugee agency envoy met Rwandan military strongman Paul Kagame on Tuesday in an attempt to defuse the eastern Zaire crisis and safeguard more than a million refugees.
Assistant High Commissioner for Refugees Sergio Vieira de Mello discussed the two-week-old fighting and the fate of refugees with Vice-President and Defence Minister Major-General Kagame.

Gerard Prunier, a French historian and expert on the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, told the British Broadcasting Corporation on Monday that Kagame held the reins of power and was essential to any successful negotiations to bring peace to eastern Zaire.
Officials said an Organisation of African Unity (OAU) peace mission led by assistant Secretary-General Anatole Tiendrebeogo would also meet Kagame separately on Tuesday in the Rwandan capital.
The OAU wants a framework for dialogue between warring sides to prevent the war from spreading in the giant African country.

"There is evidence that a lot of refugees would like to come back home. So we need to get in there (eastern Zaire) and be able to help repatriate them back home," said Paul Stromberg, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
Diplomats in Kigali said the meetings with Kagame were significant because he controls Rwanda's 54,000-strong, Tutsi-dominated army as the chairman of the high command.
"It is far more useful to meet and hold talks with Kagame on the plight of refugees than to hold conferences far away from the region. He is the key to what Rwanda does next," a diplomat said.
The talks in Kigali started as African leaders met in Nairobi to discuss the fighting between Zaire's army and Tutsi rebels and the plight of more than a million refugees caught in the war zone.
Zaire accuses Burundi, Rwanda and Uganda of backing the rebels, who in the past two weeks have seized much of eastern Zaire and a string of border cities and towns in Africa's newest civil war.
The war erupted two weeks ago when local Zairean authorities in Bukavu tried to expel ethnic Banyamulenge Tutsis from Zaire back to Rwanda -- a land they left as long ago as 200 years ago.
On Monday night, Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu made a special appeal to the refugees to return and help rebuild their ethnically-torn country and promised equality and fairness.
Rwanda like neighbouring Burundi is divided between minority Tutsis and majority Hutus. In both countries, Tutsi-dominated armies hold sway.

Refugees have been on the road since fighting erupted in eastern Zaire and aid agencies are warning of a humanitarian disaster unless aid reached them or corridors were opened to enable them return home.
"Rwanda needs all its children to achieve reconciliation and to build a beautiful country in which each has a place, each gets his share," Bizimungu, himself a Hutu, said.
Many refuse to return home for fear of reprisals for their role in the 1994 genocide and have headed deeper into Zaire.
